blocks.text: Since it appears from what has been said so far that the raven is a base and abject animal, and hateful to men, some wonder why sacred Scripture so often and so explicitly testifies that ravens are a care to God. Thus Iob. XXXIX, 3. (var. XXXVIII, 41.): Who prepares for the raven its food, when its young cry to God, wandering for lack of food? And Psal. CXLVII, (var. CXLVI,) 9. Who gives to the beasts their food, and to the young of the ravens that cry. And Luc. XII, 24: Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Nor do many of the ancients allow these passages to be understood literally. To call upon God (says Hilary on Psalm 146) is the proper office of man. But how do the young of ravens call upon God? And why the young of ravens rather than the ravens etc.? Or what food is supplied? Will God, as he gives hay to the beasts and grass to men, so bestow the stinking filth of rotting carcasses and the deaths of cattle as food for the present life on the young ravens that pray to him? To understand these things so is, I will not say an error, but the height of irreligion. And Augustine: Shall we perhaps think this, that ravens call upon God to give them food? Do not imagine this, that an irrational soul calls upon God etc. Take what is said as a figure. And the author of the Commentaries on the Psalms under the name of Jerome: Answer, Jew, answer, you who follow only the Jewish letter. Do you say these ravens are truly ravens? If then it is written of the young of ravens, „And to the young of ravens calling upon him;“ and it is written Ioel. II. ^{a)}, Whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved: then the young of ravens too will be saved in the resurrection. And so the sacred Doctors take refuge in allegories as in a sacred anchor. By ravens they understand the gentiles; by the young of ravens, Christians, who, though sprung from the gentiles, [col. 204] nevertheless call upon the true God. But, if I may say so with their leave, allegories do not destroy the literal sense but presuppose it. I would therefore not indulge in them before the literal sense is established. If we reject it in these passages, nothing in Scripture will be certain, nothing that cannot easily be twisted elsewhere. For why should we not admit that Job in chapter 39 treated of real ravens just as of real ibexes, lions, wild asses, horses, eagles, ostriches etc. in what follows or precedes in this same chapter? Since in so many descriptions of animals we freely admit that the rest are taken literally, why should this one alone contain nothing that is not allegorical? So too in these words of David, Who gives to the beasts their food, and to the young [II, 795] of the ravens that cry: since the first part of the verse signifies real beasts, why should the latter not also signify real ravens? And in Christ's words, Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap etc., that birds are meant, not men, is plainly shown 1. by comparing this passage with the parallel Matth. VI, 26. Behold the birds of the air, which do not sow, nor reap, etc. 2. Because they are denied to sow, reap and have barns into which to gather their produce. 3. Because at the end of the verse Christ adds, How much more are you worth than the birds? as in Luke; or, Are you not of much more value than they? as in Matthew. 4. Finally, if ravens or birds are understood allegorically, the lilies in what follows will not be real lilies either, but whatever it pleases τοῖς ἀλληγορηταῖς [tois allēgorētais] to invent. Let this therefore stand certain, that in the passages we have cited real ravens are meant. Nor should anyone be moved by the objection from the Psalm, τοῖς νεοσσοῖς τῶν κοράκων τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις αὐτὸν [tois neossois tōn korakōn tois epikaloumenois auton], to the young of ravens calling upon him, since the Hebrew has only that God gives his food לבני עורב אשר יקראו, to the sons of the raven, which cry. This is followed by the Chaldee, the Syriac, and Jerome's version. But, after the Greeks, the Vulgate translator, the Ethiopic, and the two Arabic versions added the pronoun, as if the Prophet had expressly said that the young of ravens call upon God, or cry to God. Yet if anyone thinks that after David's words, to the young of ravens that cry, one should supply to God, I will not strongly contest it, since in Job the young of ravens are explicitly said to cry to God: but in the sense in which young lions are said to roar after their prey, and to seek their food from God, Psal. CIV, 21; and the eyes of all animals to look to God, who gives them their food in its season, Psal. CXLV, 15; and the beasts of the field to cry out to him, because the watercourses are dried up, Ioel. I, 20. Rightly therefore Theodoret: Οὐ λογικὴ τῶν κοράκων ἡ φύσις, οὐδ᾽ ὅτι λογικῶς ἐπικαλεῖται τὸν ποιητήν· ἀλλ᾽ ἡ διὰ τὴν χρείαν κραυγὴ μιμεῖται τὴν αἴτησιν [Ou logikē tōn korakōn hē physis, oud᾽ hoti logikōs epikaleitai ton poiētēn; all᾽ hē dia tēn chreian kraugē mimeitai tēn aitēsin]. The nature of ravens is not rational, nor does it call upon its maker by the guidance of reason: but the cry uttered from need imitates a petition. Elias of Crete copied this almost word for word in his Notes on Gregory's Oration 51. And the metaphor, elegant everywhere, is the more elegant where ravens are concerned, because, while most birds seem to celebrate God with their song and to sing hymns εὐχαριστικοὺς [eucharistikous] in his praise, the raven has a clamorous and noisy voice, like an importunate beggar. And in fact it is believed sometimes to ask for alms with its croaking. Hence (as Aelian relates, History book 2, ch. 48) Κόρακες Αἰγύπτιοι, ὅσοι τῷ Νείλῳ προσδιαιτῶνται, τῶν πλεόντων ἐοίκασιν ἱκέται εἶναι, λαβεῖν τι αἰτοῦντες [Korakes Aigyptioi, hosoi tō Neilō prosdiaitōntai, tōn pleontōn eoikasin hiketai einai, labein ti aitountes], the Egyptian ravens that live along the Nile seem to be suppliants, as it were, of those sailing by, begging that something be given them. And in Hesychius: Κοράξαι, ἄγαν προσλιπαρῆσαι· πεποίηται παρὰ τοὺς κόρακας [Koraxai, agan prosliparēsai; pepoiētai para tous korakas] (I would prefer παρὰ τοῦ κόρακος [para tou korakos]). By these words he means that τὸ κοράξαι [to koraxai] is the same as to ask insistently, and that the word is taken from ravens. And Suidas under Κοράττειν [Korattein] adds the reason, saying it was taken ἀπὸ τῶν περὶ τὰς θύρας κοράκων περιπετομένων, [II, 796] καὶ μὴ ἀποχωρούντων [apo tōn peri tas thyras korakōn peripetomenōn, kai mē apochōrountōn], from ravens which (seeking something) fly around the doors of houses and do not depart from there.
